claims.text: As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has established high strength and high-temperature creep resistance.
Mo should be replaced by an equivalent atomic fraction of Nb to form equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is a documented high-entropy alloy composition.
Replacing Mo with Nb will lower the alloy density relative to HfMoTaTiZr.
The density reduction will be approximately 5–15%.
Replacing Mo with Nb will not compromise room-temperature tensile strength.
Replacing Mo with Nb will preserve creep resistance near 1000 °C.
The modified alloy will retain a homogeneous high-entropy solid-solution microstructure.
The modified alloy will retain lattice distortion similar to that of HfMoTaTiZr.
The modified alloy may retain similar precipitation behavior.
Nb has a lower density than Mo.
Nb is sufficiently chemically and structurally similar to Mo to preserve the relevant alloy behavior.
Maintaining five elements in equal atomic percentages maintains high configurational entropy.
Preserved configurational entropy and lattice distortion will maintain solid-solution strengthening.
Preserved phase stability and microstructural features will maintain high-temperature stability and creep resistance.
The proposed scope extends to tensile and creep loading at room temperature and approximately 1000 °C.
A density decrease below 5% or a greater than approximately 10% deterioration in either room-temperature tensile strength or high-temperature creep resistance will reject the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The cited record reports a density of 9.94 g/cm³ for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr. Relative to the stated 10.21 g/cm³ baseline, this is only about a 2.6% reduction, not the predicted 5–15%, and it falls below the hypothesis's own 5% minimum-density-reduction criterion.

The conditions state tensile and creep testing at both room and elevated temperatures, but the proposed experiment specifies only room-temperature tensile testing and approximately 1000 °C creep testing, leaving the other stated loading-temperature combinations untested.
